items.heading: The Definitions Come From
items.text: The definitions come from the specified-disability list under the RPwD Act. They decide what you can claim, but the working needs differ a lot inside each label.

items.heading: Rules Differ By Board
items.text: Rules differ by board and exam. This table records what the documents we read say, and where they are silent.

items.heading: Most of the Gap Between
items.text: Most of the gap between deaf students and their results is access. Ask in writing, and ask early.

visuals.heading: Deaf, Hard of Hearing: What the Labels

rows: The Act's specified-disability list defines deaf as 70 dB hearing loss in speech frequencies in both ears.
Many deaf students use Indian Sign Language (ISL) as their first language and read and write the school language as a second one.
A sign language interpreter, captions, written notes and a seat with a clear view of the speaker.
Defined as 60 dB to 70 dB hearing loss in speech frequencies in both ears.
Many use hearing aids and spoken language, and tire quickly in noise, group talk and phone calls.
A quiet seat, captions, slides and notes in advance, and meetings run one speaker at a time.
Deafened later in life, or one-sided loss
Loss that does not meet the two definitions above may not count as a benchmark disability, so check the assessment.
Needs vary a lot. Some people sign, some lip-read, some rely on devices.
Ask the medical board what your result means before you plan around a quota.
